title: How the Terracotta Army Works
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck discuss the Terracotta Army, the thousands of life-size terracotta soldiers buried with China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang (spelled Chen Shi Huangdi in the transcript), near Xi'an. They cover the 1974 discovery by farmers digging a well in Lintong, the emperor's tyrannical unification of China, his mausoleum and mercury-river legend, how the figures were made (molds for heads, hand-coiled bodies, individual faces, lacquer paint), the foremen's stamps, later smaller armies of the Han dynasty, and the unexcavated tomb's booby traps and mercury. The episode ends with listener mail about a goose named Gustavo who adopted baby ducks, and a teacher's note on using the show in class.

segments.title: Opening banter and Terracotta Army exhibit
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about the Terracotta Army exhibit travelling to museums, then joke about British beer measures and pints before starting the topic.

segments.title: 1974 well discovery and the emperor's tomb
segments.summary: Farmers digging a well in the village of Lintong hit terracotta face and head shards at about thirteen feet. Archaeologists were called and recognized the site as near the burial ground of Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor, whose funerary complex was huge and still largely unexcavated.

segments.title: Qin Shi Huang's brutal unification of China
segments.summary: The hosts describe the emperor as a tyrant who unified seven warring kingdoms, ended the practice of mass burial with the court, forced labor and relocations, burned books, executed scholars, built roads and the Great Wall, and unified money and measurements. The square coin with a round hole is described as symbolizing earth and heaven.

segments.title: Emperor's obsession with immortality and mercury
segments.summary: The emperor's paranoia about death led him to take mercury pills, to send people searching for elixirs of youth, and to execute doctors and scientists who failed to make him immortal. The hosts discuss his mausoleum and his psychology.

segments.title: Making the soldiers: crossbows and individualized figures
segments.summary: The army included bowmen and infantry, with the crossbow central to Qin military success. The figures were made partly from molds (heads and limbs) but bodies were hand-coiled, each face and hairstyle was individually made to reflect rank, and foremen's stamps indicated 83 craftsmen who could be punished for flaws.

segments.title: Painting, later armies, and the tomb's booby traps
segments.summary: The figures were originally painted and lacquered, though time and humidity have faded them. The hosts compare the Qin army to the smaller Han dynasty armies and note Sima Qian's description of the tomb with mercury rivers and a pearl constellation. Mercury levels and booby traps make excavation dangerous, and about 600 pits have been unearthed. Stats on labor, size, and weight are given.

segments.title: Han Dynasty contrast and Rodney Dangerfield tangent
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Emperor Han Jingdi's kinder rule, the Wei Shan site found in 2002, and a joking tangent about Rodney Dangerfield's epitaph. They suggest the Terracotta Army is worth searching for on the web.

segments.title: Listener mail: Gustavo the goose
segments.summary: A listener writes that a goose named Gustavo at an urban farm in Austin, Texas adopted abandoned baby ducks, and that a high school world history teacher plays episodes in class.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact info for Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website, and sign off.
